EXTRA CLASS · DOCTOR VISIT

A gentle guide for kids.

A whole check-up, one calm card at a time: the visit runs in order — getting ready, meeting the helpers, the check-up itself and after the visit — with a teddy bear on every step. Every lesson below is step by step, right on this page.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

A whole check-up, one calm card at a time.

The Doctor Visit is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for families with a check-up coming up — or with a child who asks "what happens at the doctor?" It helps children know what to expect by walking the visit in order, and a teddy bear comes along on every step: checked, weighed, listened to and proudly discharged, right beside your child.

The cards run in visit order on purpose. The gentle steps come first — the appointment, the waiting room, the helpers’ hello — and the two big ones, the x-ray and the hospital bed, arrive late, when your child already knows the story. Nothing at a check-up is a punishment: the doctor is counting what is already good, and the last card of the day is a proud wave goodbye.

From the appointment to the goodbye.

Twenty-two cards in four groups, exactly the order a check-up happens. Every step-by-step lesson is right here on this page — the original artwork beside the teaching, card after card.

THE CLASS GAME

Play doctor at home.

Let your child be the doctor and check their teddy with a toy stethoscope — hello first, then the heart listen, the ears, the big open "aah" and one deep breath. Then swap, and your child is the patient who knows exactly what each step feels like. A child in the doctor’s seat is a child who stops worrying about the waiting room.

THE ONE RULE, SAID KINDLY

Medicine is only taken from a grown-up.

The medicine card carries the rule right on its face, and the class repeats it the same way every time: grown-ups measure it, grown-ups give it — only from a grown-up. Medicine is not candy and not a toy; it lives up high, and the child’s job is the asking: "may I have my medicine, please?" Said kindly and often, the rule becomes one the child recites without being asked — which is exactly how it protects them.

Every lesson has a matching flashcard in the library: the original artwork as a printable card with a download button and short notes for grown-ups. Pack the cards for the waiting room — the visit, told in order, is the whole comfort.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 22 cards in Doctor Visit, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Doctor Visit. We have 22 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Appointment

    “Appointment! A time to visit the doctor. Look — the calendar says TODAY. We get dressed, we take teddy, and off we go!”

    How: Circle the appointment on a real calendar and let your child cross off the days. A countdown turns a surprise into a plan — and plans are what calm little worries.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Reception Desk

    “Reception desk! We tell the receptionist our name. ‘Hello, we are here!‘ She already knows — the doctor is expecting us.”

    How: Play reception at home: a toy phone, a notebook, and your child behind the "desk" saying "hello, who is here today?" — with every stuffed animal checking in by name.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Name Tag

    “Name tag! It helps people know your name. The doctor reads it: ‘Hello, Alex!‘ — and now you are friends.”

    How: Make a paper name tag together before a real visit — your child’s name, a drawing, maybe one for teddy. Wearing it in the waiting room is a small pride moment.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Waiting Room

    “Waiting room! We wait for our turn. Teddy waits too. Soon a helper will call our name — and then the visit begins!”

    How: Keep a tiny "waiting bag": one small book or quiet toy that only comes out at the clinic. Waiting with a job is easy; waiting with nothing is long.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Doctor

    “Doctor! A doctor helps you feel better. She says hello, she asks teddy how he feels, and she takes gentle care of you.”

    How: Read the doctor card, then the Class 33 community-helpers cards: the doctor at the clinic, the dentist in the chair — helpers everywhere. Name them all.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Nurse

    “Nurse! A nurse helps care for you. She knows all about bandages and kind words, and she shows the doctor how you are doing.”

    How: Play nurse with the teddy hospital: the nurse takes teddy’s temperature, wraps his paw, and says "all better." Swap roles halfway through.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Weigh-In

    “Weigh-in! Stand on the scale — click! The scale checks how much you weigh. You grew! Last time you were smaller!”

    How: Weigh the family, one by one, on the bathroom scale — including teddy. Numbers are just facts about bodies, and facts lose their scariness with practice.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Exam Room

    “Exam room! This is where check-ups happen. Sit on the big bed — boing! Teddy sits next to you. The doctor will be right in.”

    How: Arrange chairs and a couch cushion into an "exam room" for teddy. Every familiar prop at home removes one unknown at the clinic.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Check-Up

    “Check-up! A check-up keeps you healthy. The doctor listens, looks and checks — and says ‘everything is growing just right!‘”

    How: Give the teddy a full check-up in order: ears, mouth, tummy, heart. Then swap — your child is the doctor, you are the patient who sits very still.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Stethoscope

    “Stethoscope! A doctor listens to your heart. Boom-boom, boom-boom — that is YOUR heart, talking!”

    How: A toy stethoscope (or a paper tube pressed to the chest) lets your child hear a real heartbeat — yours first, then teddy’s, then their own.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Thermometer

    “Thermometer! It checks your temperature. Tick-tock, a little beep — all done! The doctor reads the number.”

    How: Check the temperature of everything: teddy (warm!), your child’s forehead, the bath water with the bath thermometer. Measuring is a game bodies love.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Ear Check

    “Ear check! The doctor looks inside your ear — a teeny light! Hold still like a statue… one… two… all done!”

    How: Play "what is in your ear?" with a flashlight at home — look in teddy’s ears, then your child’s (gently, never deep). Statues get prizes.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Mouth Check

    “Mouth check! Open wide and say AHHH. The doctor sees your teeth and your tongue — what a big open mouth!”

    How: Practice the "aah" in the mirror — the bigger the better, with a silly face at the end. Then check every stuffed animal’s mouth in the house.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Eye Chart

    “Eye chart! We read letters and pictures with our eyes. Which way does the E point? You show it with your hands!”

    How: Make a home eye chart: a heart, a star, a cup drawn on paper — "which way is the heart pointing?" Pointing games are vision checks in disguise.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Deep Breath

    “Deep breath! Breathe in and out slowly. Smell the flower… blow the candle… again! The doctor is listening to your wind.”

    How: Practice flower-and-candle breathing anywhere — in the car, at bath time. It is a check-up skill AND the classic calm-down trick in one.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · X-Ray

    “X-ray! It takes a picture inside your body. Look — those are your BONES! The camera never touches you. Click, all done.”

    How: Look at hand x-rays together (a library book or a quick print) and find the finger bones. Wave at the picture — those bones wave back.

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Medicine

    “Medicine! Take it only from a grown-up. Grown-ups measure it, grown-ups give it — and then it helps your body do its healing work.”

    How: Say the rule together at every medicine moment — the same words, every time. And keep all real medicine up high, out of small hands and out of the game.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Bandage

    “Bandage! It helps a small cut heal. Clean it, stick it on — see? The bandage is the band-aid’s job, and your body does the rest.”

    How: Bandage a teddy’s scraped paw, then let your child wear one "just because." A bandage worn proudly stops being a sign something went wrong.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Hand Washing

    “Hand washing! Clean hands help keep germs away. Soap, bubbles, scrub scrub, rinse — goodbye, germs!”

    How: Sing one whole alphabet song while washing — that is the famous twenty seconds. The clinic sink, the kitchen sink, the bathroom sink: germs lose everywhere.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Hospital Bed

    “Hospital bed! A cozy bed helps you rest. It goes UP with a button — and down! Teddy tried it. If ever someone needs it, the bed is there.”

    How: Up-and-down is the magic: a recliner chair or a stack of pillows can "be" a hospital bed for teddy. Buttons and pillows — that is the whole wonder.

  24. Cards 21–22
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Feel Better

    “Feel better! You did a great job at your check-up. You opened wide, you breathed deep, you were brave — and now, the walk home!”

    How: Invent a check-up celebration: the same song or treat after every visit. A tradition turns "the doctor" into a story with a happy ending, every time.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Goodbye

    “Goodbye! The visit is finished. Wave to the doctor — ‘bye-bye, see you next time!‘ And home you go, hand in hand.”

    How: Have the toys say goodbye after every teddy check-up — "bye-bye, Doctor!" Practiced goodbyes are easy goodbyes.

  27. 24
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  28. 25
    Check

    “Can you find Appointment? Now show me Ear Check.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  29. 26
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 22 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
